name: Visual Genome
description: Visual Genome is a dataset that connects structured image concepts to language. It contains dense annotations of objects, attributes, and relationships within each image to enable modeling of such relationships. The dataset contains over 100K images where each image has an average of 21 objects, 18 attributes, and 18 pairwise relationships between objects. All objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in region descriptions and question answer pairs are canonicalized to WordNet synsets.
creator: Ranjay Krishna, Yuke Zhu, Oliver Groth, Justin Johnson, Kenji Hata, Joshua Kravitz, Stephanie Chen, Yannis Kalantidis, Li-Jia Li, David A. Shamma, Michael S. Bernstein, Li Fei-Fei (Stanford University, Dresden University of Technology, Yahoo Inc., Snapchat Inc.)
citeAs: Ranjay Krishna et al. Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations. arXiv:1602.07332v1 [cs.CV] 23 Feb 2016
rai:dataCollection: The Visual Genome dataset uses 108,249 images from the intersection of the YFCC100M and MS-COCO datasets. These images are real-world, non-iconic images that were uploaded onto Flickr by users. The images range from as small as 72 pixels wide to as large as 1280 pixels wide, with an average width of 500 pixels. For each image, multiple region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, and question-answer pairs were collected through crowdsourcing.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Crowdsourcing
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were sourced from the intersection of YFCC100M (Thomee et al., 2016) and MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014) datasets, consisting of real-world photos uploaded to Flickr by users.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The dataset was collected over the course of 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For region descriptions: lowercase, lemmatize, and strip excess whitespace from all attributes. BLEU score thresholds set to 0.7 were used to ensure descriptions are dissimilar to previously written descriptions. For objects: Stanford's dependency parser was used to extract nouns automatically. For attributes: normalize each attribute based on morphology (stemming) and map them to WordNet adjectives. For relationships: ignore all prepositions as they are not recognized by WordNet. All components were canonicalized to WordNet synsets using word sense disambiguation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: All Visual Genome data were collected and verified entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk. For region descriptions: workers were asked to draw bounding boxes and write descriptions for regions, with explicit encouragement to write descriptions that have not been written before. For objects: workers extracted all objects from descriptions and grounded each object as a bounding box in the image. For attributes and relationships: workers were presented with region descriptions along with extracted objects and asked to add attributes to objects or connect pairs of objects with relationships. For question-answer pairs: workers wrote pairs of questions and answers about images, following rules to start questions with one of the seven Ws (who, what, where, when, why, how, which), avoid ambiguous questions, and be precise. Two types of QAs were collected: freeform QAs (8 pairs per image) and region-based QAs (based on given regions). All annotations went through a verification stage using two strategies: majority voting (three unique workers voting on correctness, requiring at least two votes for inclusion) and rapid judgments (for object verification).
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Verification was conducted using two separate strategies: majority voting (Snow et al., 2008) and rapid judgments (Krishna et al., 2016). Majority voting involved three unique workers looking at each annotation and voting on whether it is factually correct. An annotation was added to the dataset if at least two (a majority) out of the three workers verified that it is correct. Rapid judgments were used specifically to speed up the verification of objects in the dataset.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each image has an average of 42 region descriptions, 21 objects, 16 attributes, 18 relationships, and 17 question-answer pairs. For verification, 3 workers voted on each annotation using majority voting.
rai:annotatorDemographics: A total of over 33,000 unique workers contributed to the dataset. 93.02% of workers contributed from the United States, 1.29% from Philippines, 1.13% from Kenya, 0.94% from India, 0.50% from Russia, 0.47% from Canada, and 2.65% from other countries. The majority of workers were between the ages of 25 and 34 years old, with the youngest contributor being 18 years old and the oldest being 68 years old. The gender split was 54.15% male and 45.85% female workers.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford NLP tools (Manning et al., 2014) were used to extract noun phrases from region descriptions and QAs, and to extract nouns automatically from descriptions to speed up object extraction. WordNet (Miller, 1995) was used for canonicalization of objects, attributes, and relationships to synsets.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is somewhat biased towards images of people. The top synsets to which images belong include 'ski', 'ballplayer', and 'racket', all three referring to images of people playing sports. Common objects like man, person, and woman occur especially frequently with occurrences of 24K, 17K, and 11K respectively. Certain sports (skiing, surfboarding) are overrepresented due to a bias towards these sports in the source images.
rai:dataLimitations: The canonicalization mappings are not perfect and still contain some ambiguity. The precision and recall scores for canonicalization are: Objects (88.0% precision, 98.5% recall), Attributes (85.7% precision, 95.9% recall), Relationships (92.9% precision, 88.5% recall). Current models perform poorly on relationship prediction due to high intra-class variability of most relationships. The dataset's images are biased towards certain categories (e.g., people playing sports).
rai:dataUseCases: The Visual Genome dataset enables modeling of relationships between objects in images for cognitive computer vision tasks. Use cases include: training and benchmarking models for comprehensive scene understanding, dense image captioning, visual question answering, image understanding evaluation, relationship extraction, semantic image retrieval, attribute prediction, relationship prediction, and region description generation. The dataset can be used for training, testing, and validation of models.
